title: Since We Cant Agree, Lets Vote on It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article argues against a seemingly reasonable fallback for stalled team decisions: calling a vote. Its central claim is that voting, unlike consensus, permanently changes the collaborative dynamic of a team, since it teaches members they can override discussion by invoking a formal tally rather than engaging with competing arguments. Once a team votes once, the piece argues, the temptation to vote again grows, eroding the goodwill that consensus-building depends on. The recommended alternative when true consensus fails is for the leader to make the call directly, preserving the collaborative norm rather than replacing it with a democratic mechanism borrowed from governance contexts where it doesn't create the same damage.
points: Voting is framed as categorically different from consensus, not a milder version of it — one preserves collaborative norms, the other erodes them.
The erosion is self-reinforcing: once a team votes once, the likelihood of voting again (instead of working through disagreement) increases each time.
The recommended fallback when consensus fails isn't a vote but a direct leader decision, which the article argues better preserves the team's collaborative spirit.
quotes: Consensus doesn’t require that everyone agree with the decision, but it does necessitate that everyone can live with the decision and execute it as if they agreed with it.
Once a team chooses to vote on a decision, it has lost the goodwill required for consensus going forward.

Once the goodwill and collaborative spirit are broken with a vote, instead of working through tough or testy issues and decisions in the future, team members now know they can upend the process by calling for a vote, even when consensus is possible.
Voting on issues and decisions has little to recommend it in the workplace beyond expediency.
A team committed to consensus is better off allowing the leader to decide when they can’t reach a collaborative conclusion.
